title: ref, in, and out (parameter aliasing)
hook: Ordinary parameters copy data. `ref`, `in`, and `out` let a parameter alias the caller's variable instead — for writing results back, avoiding copies, or both.

sections.heading: What are ref, in, and out?

blocks.text: After you understand ordinary parameters, C# offers three **parameter modifiers** that change how data is passed. **`ref`** creates a read-write alias to the caller's variable. **`in`** creates a read-only alias (no copy for large structs). **`out`** is like `ref` but the caller may pass an unassigned variable and the callee must assign it before returning.

entries.plainDefinition: A parameter that aliases the caller's variable. Reads and writes go directly to the caller's storage.
entries.example: `void Swap(ref int a, ref int b)` — both variables are swapped in the caller.

entries.plainDefinition: A read-only alias. The callee cannot assign to the parameter. Useful for large readonly structs to avoid copying.
entries.example: `bool Contains(in CacheKey key)` — passes the key without copying.

entries.plainDefinition: An alias where the caller may pass an unassigned variable. The callee must assign a value before returning.
entries.example: `bool TryParse(string s, out int result)` — classic pattern.

entries.plainDefinition: When the compiler copies a mutable struct even through `in`, to prevent mutation via instance methods.
entries.example: Passing a mutable struct as `in` may still copy — use `readonly struct` to avoid this.

blocks.text: `out` powers the `TryParse` pattern — return a bool for success and write the parsed value through an `out` parameter. `in` avoids copying large readonly structs on hot paths like cache-key lookups. `ref` lets APIs write back to a caller's local without wrapping a one-field class. These are language features, not C++ references with destructor rules.

blocks.title: Do not cargo-cult ref on classes
blocks.body: Class parameters already pass a reference. Adding `ref` to a class parameter does not make it faster — it only forces the caller to write `ref` at the call site.

items.title: Start with ordinary parameters
items.body: Default passing is correct for most APIs. Only reach for modifiers when you have a specific reason.

items.title: Use `out` for Try-style results
items.body: The caller may pass an unassigned local. The callee must assign before return. Good APIs assign a default on failure.

items.title: Use `in` for large readonly structs
items.body: Avoids copying on every call. Pair with `readonly struct` so the compiler does not make a defensive copy.

items.title: Use `ref` for two-way aliasing
items.body: Caller must pass a definitely assigned variable and write `ref` at the call site. Properties cannot be passed as `ref` or `out`.

blocks.title: Aliasing in C# vs JS/TS
rows: Return an object `{ ok, value }` or a tuple array
No value types — objects are always references

blocks.title: ref on reference types for performance
blocks.body: Classes are already passed by reference. Adding `ref` to a class parameter does not reduce allocations or improve speed.

blocks.title: Properties are not ref locations
blocks.body: You cannot pass `obj.Count` as `ref` or `out` because a property is not a storage location — it is a method call disguised as field access.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: `in` avoids copying large readonly structs on hot paths — pair with `readonly struct` or the compiler may emit defensive copies for mutable structs. `ref readonly` returns (C# 7.2+) expose struct slots without copy — used in span-like APIs. `out` is the definite-assignment contract the compiler tracks — TryParse patterns rely on it. Never add `ref` to class parameters for performance — references already alias. Benchmark before ref-chasing; often readonly struct plus in beats ref on micro-benchmarks that lie about inlining.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Cannot pass properties — not a storage location
Caller may pass uninitialized — compiler tracks
Module 17 span patterns build on this

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Using ref on class parameters for speed. Passing a property as out. Not knowing in can still copy mutable structs. Saying JavaScript has out parameters.

interviewTakeaways: ref aliases both ways; in is readonly alias; out must be assigned by callee.
in plus mutable struct can defensive-copy — prefer readonly struct.
Properties are not ref-capable storage locations.
60s: Ordinary params copy struct. ref/in/out alias. in for large readonly struct. out for TryParse. ref on class is not a perf trick.
Follow-up: what is ref readonly return used for?
commonPitfalls: ref on reference types as cargo-cult performance gets you rejected.
Passing obj.Count as ref — properties are not locations.
Strong answer: 'in skips copy for readonly struct. out is definite assignment. ref on class adds nothing. Properties cannot be ref.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript always passes object references and copies primitives. There is no `out` or `in`. Multiple outputs use objects or arrays.
TypeScript and JavaScript prefer returning a tuple or Result object. C# still uses `out` in the Base Class Library (BCL) like `TryParse`, and tuples when you want two values without aliasing.
